title: Crossed treble — the reverse-order X-stitch
subtitle: Work the second treble before the first so it crosses in front
excerpt: Crossed treble makes a simple X-shape by working two trebles in reverse order. The second stitch is worked first, then the first stitch is worked so it crosses in front. The result is a neat interlocking pattern used in lace panels and Victorian edgings.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776 — crossed stitch patterns in open-work crochet. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Vol. 4 (1889) — crossed treble in lace panels.

glossaryTerms.definition: Two trebles worked in reverse order so the second crosses in front of the first. Work a treble into the stitch one ahead, then reach back and work a treble into the skipped stitch. The two stitches form an X.

heroPrompt: A close-up swatch of crossed treble stitch in navy DK cotton, four rows, showing the interlocking X-stitch pattern clearly, good side light on a pale linen background.

inlineDiagramTopics.description: Reaching back over the completed first stitch to work the second into the skipped stitch — the cross formation

content.text: makes an X by swapping the order of two trebles. Skip the next stitch, work a treble into the stitch after it, then reach back and work a treble into the stitch you skipped. The second stitch crosses in front of the first. Repeated across a row, crossed trebles create an interlocked diagonal X texture.
Work to the two stitches where the cross will go.
Skip the next stitch. Yarn over and work a complete treble into the stitch after the skipped one.
Yarn over and work a complete treble into the skipped stitch — inserting the hook from the front, passing it behind the treble just made.
The two trebles now cross: the second one comes in front of the first. One crossed treble pair made.
Continue: skip the next stitch, tr in stitch after, tr in skipped stitch.

attrs.title: Keeping the stitch count even
attrs.body: Crossed trebles work in pairs over 2 stitches. Your total stitch count must be even for the pattern to work out evenly. An odd stitch count at the start leaves a lone stitch at the end of each row.

items.symptom: The cross lies behind instead of in front
items.cause: Working the second treble with the hook passing in front of the first instead of behind
items.fix: When working into the skipped stitch, push the hook under the first treble from the front — through the back of the work and out — so the second treble sits in front.

items.symptom: Work becomes uneven after a few rows
items.cause: Working crossed treble pairs across an odd number of stitches
items.fix: Check your stitch count before starting the pattern. Cross trebles use stitches in pairs — you need an even total.

content.text: Crossed double treble is the taller version — the same X-stitch but with dtr, making a more pronounced cross. Both stitches appear in Victorian open-lace panels where crossed groups alternate with chain spaces.
